title: Monday Night Football: Falcons run over Saints 45-24 to ruin New Orleans' celebration
description: Bijan Robinson and Brian Robinson combined for 207 rushing yards and five touchdowns.
fullText:
The Saints will always have the Hurricane Katrina game on Sept. 25, 2006. Steve Gleason's block of a Falcons' punt is commemorated in a statue outside the Superdome titled "Rebirth."

But Monday night belonged to the Falcons.

Atlanta ruined New Orleans' "Domecoming" celebration, routing the Saints 45-24.

The Superdome cleared out in the second half as the Falcons ran over the Saints, with 205 of their 420 yards coming on the ground. Bijan Robinson had 19 carries for 145 yards and two touchdowns, and Brian Robinson added 14 carries for 62 yards and three touchdowns.

Bijan Robinson went 59 yards for a touchdown on the third play from scrimmage, a foreshadowing of how the night was going to go.

The Falcons led 14-0 at the end of the first quarter and 24-7 at halftime before continuing to pour on the points in the second half.

The Falcons scored the fewest points in the NFL the first two weeks, with 16. In the past two games, since quarterback Michael Penix returned, the Falcons have an NFL-leading 80 points. The Falcons are 2-2 and tied with the Panthers atop the NFC South. The Saints are 1-3.

Penix went 15-of-20 for 223 yards and a touchdown, which was a 31-yard throw to Jahan Dotson. Drake London caught five passes for 96 yards and Dotson had two for 54.

Alvin Kamara turned back time in scoring two of the Saints' touchdowns on runs of 3 and 5 yards. He tied Deuce McAllister's franchise record for most multiple-rushing touchdown games with his 14th.

Late in the fourth quarter, with the game out of reach, Devaughn Vele made one of the best catches of the season. He got both feet down for a 3-yard touchdown with 1:13 left.

Tyler Shough went 30-of-48 for 286 yards and a touchdown despite banging up his left hand. Chris Olave caught eight passes for 116 yards before taking a hard hit on his knee late in the game.

The only bad news for the Falcons was the loss of edge rusher Za'Darius Smith (concussion) and left tackle Jake Matthews (groin). They left in the first half with their injuries and now have a short week to try to get back for the Ravens on Sunday Night Football.

title: Instant Analysis: Falcons pummel Saints on Monday Night Football
description: Atlanta crushes New Orleans in prime-time at the Superdome
fullText:
The Cooper Rush era feels like a million years ago, because these Atlanta Falcons are a completely different football team than they were in Weeks 1-2. Tonight's dominant 45-24 victory over the New Orleans Saints puts them at 2-2 on the year, tying the Carolina Panthers at the top of the NFC South and effectively hitting the reset button for their season.

Let's review how things went in all three phases for yet another impressive showing from the Falcons under the lights.

It took less than 90 seconds for the Falcons to score their first points of the game, as running back Bijan Robinson got things started with a blazing 59-yard touchdown run on just the third play from scrimmage. Atlanta stuck with the ground game most of the night, with Robinson getting a heavy workload as well as a healthy amount of carries for backup Brian Robinson Jr.. It worked out pretty well, as they combined for 207 yards and five touchdowns on the ground, averaging 6.3 yards per carry.

The passing game was not quite as explosive as it was last week in Green Bay, but Michael Penix still looked pretty sharp in his second start of the 2026 campaign. His connection with wide receiver Drake London (five catches, 96 yards) is the most promising thing he has going for him, and Penix also managed to get tight end Kyle Pitts finally involved, offensively. Penix also got Jahan Dotson his first touchdown in a Falcons uniform. He finished the night 15/20 for 223 yards, no interceptions, one touchdown and a 127.7 passer rating.

Atlanta's NFL-best rushing defense continues to crush their opponents' attempts to get going on the ground. It didn't help that the Saints were missing their starting running back Travis Etienne, but they were held to just 50 rushing yards total and averaged a measly 2.6 yards per carry.

As for the Falcons pass rush, things continue to go swimmingly even without starting edge rushers Jalon Walker and James Pearce. Atlanta was able to generate consistent pressure on Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, who had to throw on the run a lot. While they only got to him for two sacks, the Falcons landed 12 QB hits, with Yasir Abdullah tallying a team-high four. One possible hiccup was the injury to Za'Darius Smith, who left the game early with a concussion.

The short-handed secondary was far from perfect, giving up big statlines to wide receivers Chris Olave (eight catches, 116 yards) and Devaugh Vele (six catches, 54 yards, one TD) but there was no obvious weak link in coverage like Mike Hughes was last week against the Packers. Rookie linebacker Harold Perkins Jr. continues to flash in coverage, as well.

With the offensive and defensive units dominating, there wasn't much for the Falcons special teams unit to do, tonight. Jake Bailey only had to punt the ball twice, totaling 72 yards, while Nick Folk made his one field goal attempt from 29 yards out. Once again the most-exciting element here was rookie receiver Zachariah Branch showing his potential as a return specialist, totaling 25 yards on a punt return and 65 yards total on three kickoff returns.

title: NI make huge strides despite Georgia frustration
description: With eight points from four games, Northern Ireland show real progress through what manager Michael O'Neill calls "one of the most enjoyable windows" he has had in international football.
fullText:
Northern Ireland's first nine points in the Uefa Nations League were accumulated over the grand total of 17 games.

Finishing their four-game window with a stalemate against Georgia on Monday night ensured Michael O'Neill's side earned eight across a mere 11 days.

It says plenty about the growing mood around this young side that, even after what was undoubtedly their best ever Nations League window, fans filed out of Windsor Park frustrated that it was not more.

Isaac Price's saved penalty in the 83rd minute was naturally the most glaring missed opportunity to take all three points in a second consecutive goalless draw in Belfast after Hungary also left with a point last week.

There had been other good chances, though, with Paddy Kelly and Josh Magennis both unable to capitalise on promising positions, while Ruairi McConville hit the bar in the incident that led to the penalty.

Magennis himself summed up the general mood at the final whistle when he told BBC Sport NI he was "bitterly disappointed" to take only a point from the game.

When the dust settles, however, the block as a whole can only be considered a success.

Two weeks ago, Northern Ireland were yet to win a game in the second tier of the Nations League and had never picked up all three points on their travels at any level of the competition.

Away victories in Georgia and against Ukraine in Slovakia both felt like huge steps forward for a side whose average age was as low as 22 in the latter fixture which they won 3-0.

On top of that, four successive clean sheets ensured they are the only team in the competition yet to concede a goal, all the more impressive considering that Conor Bradley remains on the sidelines and Daniel Ballard was only fit to feature in the first game.

"It was a hard camp, a lot different to what any of us have experienced before, and I thought we dealt with it really well," said Fulham midfielder Shea Charles who, along with Trai Hume, displayed Premier League pedigree throughout the window.

"We've won two away games, drew two at home, no goals conceded, there's not many complaints. I think we've been really good."

With this new four-game window presenting something different for managers across Europe to tackle, a myriad of approaches emerged.

Germany boss Jurgen Klopp named virtually two separate squads for his side's two pairs of games, while Ukraine made 10 changes between their first two games and then nine for their defeat by Northern Ireland.

Having spoken before the start of the campaign about how the condensed schedule would be more difficult for smaller nations, O'Neill kept changes to a minimum.

He started only 15 different players across the four games with two of his changes enforced by Ballard's injury and Ethan Galbraith's absence against Ukraine to attend the birth of his child.

Despite the relatively small pool of starters, this still feels like a window when Northern Ireland's depth was tested and passed with flying colours.

O'Neill was without talisman Bradley and the reliable Ali McCann coming into the window, and then lost Ballard to a hamstring injury after the first game in Tbilisi.

Young centre-backs McConville, 21, and Tom Atcheson, 20, looked ready to play at this level, while Ciaron Brown started all four games and drew plaudits having often had to bide his time in past squads.

Kieran Morrison, Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer all impressed when given a chance against Ukraine.

O'Neill's praise for his squad is across the board.

"For me it's been one of the most enjoyable windows I've had as an international manager, and that's been because of the players," said O'Neill.

"How they've applied themselves, how desperate they are to do well, that's a real positive.

"We've a brilliant group of players and a lot of them I think will play international football for a long time."

Despite what will feel like two points dropped against Georgia, the team remains top of Group B2 before next month's concluding fixtures at home to Ukraine and away to Hungary.

Having already secured their League B status at the very least, back-to-back Nations League promotions and second seeding in December's Euro 2028 qualifying draw remain on the table.

In a broader sense, the past 11 days have served to heighten the growing excitement around the team's direction of travel.

"Honestly, the sky's the limit," said Magennis.

"I think they've probably got maybe four tournaments to have a crack at. The group's in a fantastic place."

If O'Neill was slightly more coy, he echoed the general sentiment.

"I know what the potential of this team is, I'm not always going to share that with you guys if I'm honest," concluded the manager.

"For me the team is maturing and growing and progressing all the time. It's good that the fans are excited, that's what we want. We want them to look at this team and be proud.

"I know these boys over the last two or three years, I've seen them grow. I see them with each other, which is really important and this team shows all the best sides of Northern Ireland."

“Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.
fullText:
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army officer and psychiatrist who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday.

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell announced. "He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack.

"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution," he continued. "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come."

If Hasan's execution is indeed carried out by a firing squad, it would mark the first such case for the service since Jan. 31, 1945, when Pvt. Eddie D. Slovik was executed by a U.S. Army firing squad in France for desertion during World War II.

The last death sentence carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging at the gallows in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill a young girl.

Hasan, who was born in northern Virginia, walked into a Fort Hood readiness processing center on Nov. 5, 2009, and opened fire using a semi-automatic handgun.

Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier.

Former Army Staff Sgt. Patrick Zeigler, a two-time combat veteran, was shot four times in the attack and spent nearly a year recovering in various hospitals.

"He looked me straight in the eyes as he pointed the gun at me, and a split second later, I'm on the floor with a hole in my head," he told the Killeen Daily Herald in 2023.

At his court-martial, Hasan, now 56, admitted to the shooting, and in 2013 said he carried out the attack in support of the Taliban.

At the time, Hasan requested a delay in court proceedings so he could ready a new legal strategy that would show he acted "in defense of others."

Asked by presiding Judge Col. Tara Osborn who he was defending, Hasan replied, "The leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban."

Hasan was convicted by a military jury in August 2013, which recommended he be sentenced to death.

He was subsequently transferred to Fort Leavenworth, where he has been incarcerated on death row.

Jonathan Lehrfeld contributed to this report.

title: ‘Ban the frats’: Protests erupt at Cornell over handling of rape allegation
description: Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration at Cornell.Photograph: Olga...
fullText:
Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials' handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president's resignation and painting "SMASH THE PATRIARCHY" on an administration building.

Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.

Protesters shouted, "Ban the frats" and held signs saying, "At Cornell, rapists are safer than women" and "Stop rape culture." Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell's president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting, "Kotlikoff, resign!"

The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president's office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported.

The messages in red paint read "SMASH THE PATRIARCHY" and "AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED". The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.

The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting "the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place".

"We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell's administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual," the statement added. The students' painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.

Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.

"We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer," Kimball said. "We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law."

The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. "We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape," they wrote. "Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is."

The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe's case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.

According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.

A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.

Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write "reflection papers".

The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were "afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell".

The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.

One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said: "Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?"

And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: "Rape should not be inevitable."

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office's handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were "dramatically different" from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe's attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.

Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state's attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.

Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included "a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life", Kotlikoff said.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

fullText:
GRAND ISLAND, Nebraska, Oct 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday to expand access to tax-exempt diesel that ‌he unveiled from a rally stage in Nebraska.

High diesel prices, which shot to a ‌record of about $6.50 a gallon last month, are a risk to Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm US elections ​in which control of Congress is at stake. Trump's Republican Party currently holds a narrow majority in the Senate and House of Representatives.

Prices for the fuel integral to trucking goods have risen in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with the conflicts having led to ‌attacks on refineries in the Middle ⁠East and Russia.

Trump said the directive will waive the off-road requirement for tax-free diesel and allow anyone to buy the red dye diesel fuel that ⁠is used by the agriculture industry and by some off-road vehicles.

"We are not going to need it long, I hope," Trump said of the waiver.

The order released by the White House directs the treasury secretary, in ​consultation ​with the Pentagon chief, "to defer payment of the federal ​excise tax imposed for on-road use of ‌dyed diesel fuel for the remainder of the year without interest or penalties, and to explore pathways to eliminate the obligation to pay the deferred taxes."

It also directs the US agriculture secretary to "ensure farmers' access to dyed diesel in high-demand areas" while asking the transportation secretary to coordinate with states, industry leadership, and labor organizations on access to dyed diesel.

G7 countries announced last week that they ‌would release 100 million barrels of diesel, after pressure ​from Trump who had considered banning US exports of the ​fuel. But it was not clear how ​much of that release would be entirely new supplies or compliance with a ‌global agreement in March.

Trump's approval rating held ​at a record-low 32% ​in recent days, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday, with Americans most concerned about the high cost of living, spurred by soaring gasoline and diesel prices due to the ​US war on Iran.

fullText:
Russia on Monday sought to downplay reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help.

Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.

"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.

"We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can."

The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.

But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".

He said on Telegram that Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".

He added that there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the woman's death.

Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "stable".

"The situation remains under our control and that of the experts."

Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements rather than... rumours and speculations".

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.

The reports will be closely watched in Washington, where memories of the Covid-19 pandemic that started in Trump's first term are still fresh.

Trump has strongly backed the theory that the disease was due to a leak from a laboratory in Wuhan, China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said his country was monitoring the Russia situation but saw no "cause for alarm".

"There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread," Rubio told reporters before taking off for a visit to Iceland.

"So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we're doing that."

Experts said the reported response in Russia appeared "proportionate".

"It appears that measures are being implemented to quarantine any potential contacts and prevent any onward transmission," Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology, Imperial College London, said in a commentary.

description:

Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. 
In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term.

In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations.

"I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far."

He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say."

Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically.

Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent."

At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass."

Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections.

"All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes.

The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way."

Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie.

On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result."

On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor.

"I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes.

If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape."

He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his " Big Beautiful Bill " of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done."

"Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes.

He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT."

In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults.

Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response.

"I care if you fail and right now we are failing," Tillis wrote to Trump.
